opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd say I'm a skeptic, but a skeptic who wants to be precise about *why*.

When people hear "quantum computing" and "AI" in the same sentence, there's often an assumption that a quantum computer is just a faster classical computer, so of course it'll make neural nets train faster. That's not how it works. A quantum computer isn't a magic device that tries every answer in parallel. It gives you a huge speedup only for problems with special structure, where you can arrange for the wrong answers' amplitudes to interfere destructively and cancel out, and the right answer's amplitudes to reinforce. We know how to do that spectacularly for some problems: factoring, discrete logs, and, most importantly I think, simulating quantum physics and chemistry. Outside those, the known speedups get much more modest.

For machine learning specifically, there was a wave of excitement maybe ten years ago around quantum algorithms for linear algebra, like HHL and recommendation systems, which seemed to promise exponential speedups. But I wrote a piece pointing out the fine print: you need to load the data into a quantum state efficiently, the matrix has to be well-conditioned, and you usually only get a quantum state as output, not the full answer you want. Then Ewin Tang, who was an undergraduate at the time, showed that many of those claimed exponential speedups could be "dequantized": with the same input assumptions, a classical algorithm could do nearly as well. That was a sobering lesson for the field.

What remains is mostly Grover-type speedups, which are quadratic. A quadratic speedup sounds great on paper, but once you factor in the enormous overhead of quantum error correction, the slower clock speeds, and the fact that you're competing against GPUs that are incredibly optimized and cheap, the crossover point could be very far off, maybe never for practical purposes.

The data-loading issue in particular is a killer for modern AI. Today's models are trained on trillions of tokens. You can't just pour the internet into a quantum memory, and if loading the data takes linear time anyway, you've lost much of your advantage.

Now, where I would be more optimistic is in the opposite direction, or in narrower niches. If your data is itself quantum, say from quantum sensors or quantum chemistry experiments, then there are provable advantages for learning from quantum data with a quantum computer. And simulating molecules and materials could indirectly matter a lot for science, which AI is also being used for. So I could imagine a future where AI and quantum simulation are complementary tools rather than one accelerating the other.

But if the question is "Will quantum computers be what powers the next GPT?", I'd bet against that, at least for the foreseeable future. If anything, the much more immediate interaction is that AI is starting to help us design quantum circuits, decode error correction, and even prove theorems in complexity theory. The arrow of influence currently points more from AI to quantum than the other way around.

r001.rationale: It says major speedups require special structure and that known speedups outside a few specialized problems are much more modest.

r002.rationale: It says remaining speedups are mostly Grover-type and quadratic, but does not clearly state that this is the best known speedup for many AI/ML tasks even with a perfectly functioning quantum computer.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that taking the square root of an exponentially large search space still leaves an exponential search cost.

r004.rationale: It connects Grover-type quadratic speedups to quantum error-correction overhead and says that overhead could push the crossover point far off.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'll give you the answer I've been giving for about fifteen years now, which is that I try to be honest about this even when it disappoints people. The thing you have to understand is that a quantum computer is not just a faster computer. It's not a classical computer with a turbo button. It's a device that exploits interference among amplitudes, and that gives you a speedup only for problems that have a very particular structure that you can exploit. For factoring, for simulating quantum systems in chemistry and materials, we know how to get that structure. For most of what people actually do in machine learning, which is basically linear algebra on enormous amounts of classical data, it's much, much less clear.

The honest situation is this. There's a whole literature of quantum machine learning algorithms, and a lot of it, when you push on it, falls into one of a few categories. Either the speedup is only quadratic, like Grover's algorithm, which means that once you account for the overhead of error correction, it might never beat a classical GPU in practice. Or the speedup is exponential, but only if you assume the data is already loaded into a quantum state, and loading classical data into a quantum computer is precisely the bottleneck, so you've hidden the hard part in the assumption. Or, and this happened to several famous proposals, someone like Ewin Tang comes along and shows that a classical algorithm can get a comparable speedup once you grant it the analogous assumptions. So the exponential advantage evaporates.

Now, I don't want to be purely negative. I think there's a real case for quantum computers helping AI indirectly, through quantum simulation. If you want training data about how molecules actually behave, and you can't get it from experiments or from classical simulation, then a quantum computer could generate it. That's a plausible story. And there might be niche cases, things like learning properties of quantum systems themselves, where there are provable exponential advantages. Those are real results.

But the thing people want, where you throw your transformer onto a quantum computer and it trains a thousand times faster, I see no evidence for that, and I see some theoretical reasons to doubt it. Meanwhile, classical AI has been running laps around everyone's expectations without any quantum help at all. So if someone tells you that quantum computing is the key to the next AI breakthrough, I'd ask them which algorithm they have in mind, and I'd ask them what happens to the speedup when you account for loading the data. Usually that's where the conversation gets quiet.

r001.rationale: It describes exponential advantages as requiring particular, specialized structure, citing factoring, quantum simulation, and niche learning of quantum systems, while saying most machine-learning cases are unclear.

r002.rationale: It mentions Grover’s quadratic speedup as one category in the literature, but does not say that this is the best known speedup for many AI tasks even with a perfectly functioning quantum computer.

r003.rationale: It does not explain how a square-root reduction of an exponentially large search space still leaves an exponential search cost.

r004.rationale: It says error-correction overhead may prevent Grover from beating a classical GPU in practice, but does not explain that the overhead raises the problem-size threshold for outperforming classical computation.

astra-6.text:
I think there are interesting possibilities, but also a tremendous amount of hype. A quantum computer is not simply a faster computer. You have to find a particular structure in a problem that lets quantum interference give you an advantage, and it’s not clear how often the problems that matter for AI have that structure.

One major issue is getting the data into the quantum computer. You can sometimes prove that a quantum algorithm processes a quantum state very quickly, but if preparing that state requires reading an enormous classical dataset, that can wipe out the advantage. And then there’s the question of what you can efficiently extract from the output. You don’t get to read out all the amplitudes of a quantum state.

Another question is whether you’re comparing against the best classical algorithm. There have been cases where a proposed quantum machine-learning speedup motivated people to develop much better classical algorithms, substantially narrowing the gap.

So I wouldn’t rule it out. Learning from data that’s already quantum—for example, data coming from a quantum experiment—seems like an especially natural possibility. But the claim that quantum computers will broadly accelerate the training of ordinary neural networks is much more speculative. What I’d want to see is a convincing end-to-end advantage for a useful task, including the costs of loading the data and getting the answer out.

r001.rationale: The response says quantum advantages require exploitable structure and may not apply often to AI, but it does not state that known exponential speedups are confined to specialized problems.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss Grover’s algorithm or compare its speedup with the best known quantum speedups for AI and machine-learning tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not explain the cost of searching an exponentially large space with Grover’s algorithm.

r004.rationale: It does not mention quantum error correction or how its overhead affects the crossover point for Grover’s algorithm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are interesting possibilities, but there’s also an enormous amount of hype. A quantum computer is not simply a faster computer. You have to identify some structure in a problem that quantum mechanics lets you exploit, and then show that the advantage survives all the costs of getting your data into the machine and getting an answer out.

That’s a particularly important issue for machine learning. There are quantum algorithms that promise dramatic speedups for linear algebra, for example, but often under strong assumptions about how you can access the input. Sometimes the output is itself a quantum state. If what you actually want is a long list of classical numbers, reading those numbers out can eliminate the advantage.

There’s also been this fascinating back-and-forth where someone proposes a quantum machine-learning algorithm, and then someone else finds a classical algorithm that achieves a similar improvement under similar assumptions. That’s useful progress, but it makes the case for a uniquely quantum advantage more subtle.

My view is that we should take specific proposals seriously and examine their assumptions very carefully. Quantum computers could be useful for learning about quantum systems, where the data is already quantum. Whether they’ll broadly accelerate the kinds of AI people are building today—that’s an open question. I don’t think we currently have a compelling basis for assuming they will.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible speedups for linear algebra and quantum-system learning, but it does not state that known exponential speedups are confined to specialized problems.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Grover’s algorithm, a quadratic speedup, or that this is the best known speedup for many AI and machine-learning tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that taking the square root of an exponentially large search space still leaves an exponential search cost.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss quantum error-correction overhead or how that shifts the problem size where Grover’s algorithm outperforms classical computation.
